The Big Story · Space

Japan is flying five years for ten grams.

At 4:41:03 a.m. on Tuesday, Japan plans to launch MMX toward Phobos. The sample it brings home could reveal whether Mars captured a wandering asteroid—or built a moon from the wreckage of an ancient collision.

Diplomacy · Shinjuku

International cooperation moves into a city plaza

Global Festa Japan opened today across Shinjuku Sumitomo Building’s Sankaku Hiroba and Shinjuku Central Park. The 35th edition runs from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. on October 17 and 18 and combines in-person exhibits with online stages. It is co-hosted by Japan’s Foreign Ministry, JICA and the Japan NGO Center for International Cooperation.

The theme—“Connected to the World, My Everyday Life”—tries to make development policy tangible. Programs connect food, travel, games and ordinary shopping choices to overseas cooperation. One stage uses Momotaro Dentetsu World, a familiar railway-board-game series, to introduce ODA sites; another follows the route from a meal to children’s futures. Performers, NGO workers and development specialists share the schedule rather than separating policy into a closed conference.

For visitors, the practical distinction is location. Indoor programs are at Shinjuku Sumitomo Building’s triangular atrium; outdoor activity is across the street in Shinjuku Central Park’s Fun More Time Hiroba. Participation is free, and the official site carries a live stream for people outside Tokyo. Today’s opening is not a new Japanese aid pledge. It is a public-facing event that shows how the government and civil society explain existing international cooperation to a domestic audience. The 35-year history also matters: the fair turns organizations normally encountered through reports and donation pages into people a visitor can question directly. Sunday remains a full second day, so October 17 is the opening rather than the entire event today.

Health · Nationwide

A medicine-awareness week begins with a practical warning

Japan’s Health Ministry began its annual Medicine and Health Week today. The October 17–23 campaign is organized with prefectures, the Japan Pharmaceutical Association and regional pharmacist groups. Its purpose is not to advertise a particular drug: it is to improve public understanding of correct medicine use and of the professional role pharmacists play in preventing harm.

This year’s official information points readers toward verified pharmacy listings, electronic prescriptions and electronic medicine notebooks, as well as guidance on personal imports and blood donation. Those topics matter because medicine safety often fails outside the moment of prescription—when products are stored incorrectly, combined without advice, bought through an uncertain online seller, or used after a patient forgets what another clinic supplied.

The government calendar explains why the week always begins on October 17: the date is associated with Yakusojin-sai, a festival honoring deities connected with medicine. The historical reference now supports a modern safety campaign. A television-drama tie-in with WOWOW’s MR: Medical Representative also explains how medicines move from manufacturers toward patients and how efficacy and safety are managed. The useful action is simple: keep an accurate list of what you take and ask a pharmacist when products overlap. This item is general public information, not individual medical advice. Anyone facing a suspected overdose, severe reaction or urgent symptom should use emergency services instead of waiting for a campaign consultation. For ordinary questions, bring the package or medicine notebook so a pharmacist can identify the exact product and dose.

Travel · Narita

The airport lost-and-found desk now starts with a chat

Narita International Airport’s official lost-property route now begins with “find chat.” A traveler chooses the relevant facility, authenticates through a message link and describes the missing item in a guided conversation. Requests can be submitted 24 hours a day; human operator responses run from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., with late-night inquiries answered the following day.

The important catch is geography. Narita divides responsibility among terminals, airlines, police and operators, and the chat does not cover every secure area. The airport explicitly excludes some spaces after international security screening and before immigration. Travelers who lost something aboard an aircraft should still contact the airline, while people needing phone assistance can call the airport’s 24-hour information number.

The service reflects a wider operational problem hidden behind the familiar image of Japan’s meticulous lost-and-found culture. A large airport receives descriptions in different languages and must match color, brand, location and time across separate custodians. A structured chat can reduce repeated calls and turn a vague report into searchable attributes. It cannot guarantee recovery, and it is not an emergency channel, but it gives an overseas visitor a documented first step before language and time-zone differences make the search harder. Include the terminal, approximate time, nearby shop or gate, distinguishing marks and a photo when available. Do not publish passport numbers or other sensitive details on social media; use the airport’s official form or phone route.

What to watch · Space

The launch window has a precise first second—and a long backup

H3 Flight 10 is scheduled for 4:41:03 a.m. JST on October 20 from Tanegashima Space Center. The precision is not decorative: launch teams calculate a time window that places MMX onto the required interplanetary path. If weather, range safety or hardware conditions prevent liftoff, JAXA lists a reserve period from October 21 through November 7, with a time assigned separately for each possible day.

The spacecraft’s first destination is not Mars’s surface but the Martian moon Phobos. MMX is designed to enter the Mars region in 2027, observe Phobos from quasi-satellite orbits, deploy the French-German IDEFIX rover, land the main craft and collect at least ten grams of material. Departure is planned for 2030 and Earth return for 2031. Those dates are targets, not completed milestones.

Viewers should distinguish the launch broadcast from the full mission. A clean ascent and separation would open the journey; it would not prove the sampling or return phases. JAXA’s official MMX gallery provides a current mission movie, photographs of the actual spacecraft and a press kit. The October 20 live coverage will show the first minutes of a chain that must remain intact for five years. The question to watch on launch morning is therefore narrow but essential: did H3 place MMX on the path from which every later operation becomes possible? The scheduled time is in Japan Standard Time; overseas viewers should convert from UTC+9 and recheck the official countdown before watching because launch times can change. If October 20 slips, the reserve window—not an old social post—is the authoritative guide.

Japanese word of the day探査 · たんさ · tansa

Exploration, investigation or probing. 探 means “to search” or “seek,” while 査 means “to examine.” Together they describe a deliberate search that gathers evidence. The word appears often in science and news, but it is not limited to space: police can conduct an underwater search, and researchers can investigate underground resources.

In today’s story, uchū tansa (宇宙探査) means space exploration, kasei tansa (火星探査) means Mars exploration, and a probe is a tansaki (探査機)—literally an “exploration machine.” MMX is a kasei eisei tansaki, a Martian-moon exploration spacecraft.

A natural example is: MMX wa Kasei no eisei o tansa shimasu—“MMX will explore the moons of Mars.” The verb form is 探査する, “to explore or investigate.” The nuance is useful: MMX is not merely traveling somewhere. It will observe, measure, land, sample and return evidence. That full chain is why 探査 is today’s precise word. Learn vocabulary in motion with DraMap for iOS.
